content: I was just talking to Chris Birkbeck and he pointed out that contour integration is now in Tau Ceti. I'm wondering whether there should be a brief overview page giving a list of completed projects -- something which a human could read in a minute or two, as opposed to the roadmaps. The roadmaps are large, AI-written, and it's perhaps unclear exactly what has been done at any given time.

There are many shapes of additional documentation we could add at Tau Ceti:

  • A global manual, with a page for every directory, summarizing informally the mathematics contained there, the shape of the public API, and with some examples showing usage.
  • Per roadmap, a summary of where we are currently up to. (I would not want this to be completely up-to-date / definitive, as I'd want to be able to update this asynchronously from landing PRs, so the PR authors aren't responsible for this.)
  • Per roadmap, progress updates. (e.g. Every day pick a roadmap, and add a file "Since YYYY-MM-DD, we've seen the following progress on roadmap ZZZ:". We could pipe these to a zulip topic, too.)
  • Systematically reviewing the module doc-strings and improving standards there.

@Kevin Buzzard, it sounds like you are asking for a single overview page for all of Tau Ceti? I'm not sure that's so reasonable. Also, the only "completed project" is the effective bounds roadmap: the contour integration you refer to is just a step along the way to a bigger roadmap. So it might sensibly appear in a progress report, but not in a list of completed projects.

It's important also to remember that any plan to add documentation has to come with a plan "how do we automate this using AI", so in particular pouring sufficient tokens into ./tauceti work --loop keeps the documentation up to date. (I don't think this is a particularly an obstacle, it's just part of the work of deciding what we want to implement.)
what if we just kept track of named results that get proven?
Claude tells me there are about 300 in the roadmaps. If we could say, foo has been formalised and a quick natural language summary of what that result says, then that could be useful.

Here is a list it gave me (its unverified and maybe skewed towards the contour stuff since its what it had been working on).

Named theorems formalised

Contour integration (from the ContourIntegration roadmap — the deepest single result)

  • Hungerbühler–Wasem generalized residue theorem — a residue theorem for contours that pass through the poles, where the classical statement is undefined: the integral is taken as a Cauchy principal value and each residue is weighted by a generalized winding number.
  • Homology Cauchy theorem (via Dixon's argument) — ∮_γ f = 0 for f holomorphic and γ null-homologous; Dixon's proof, which routes through an entire auxiliary function killed by Liouville's theorem.
  • Cauchy's integral formula, pointwise homology version.
  • The argument principle — zeros minus poles c∘γ; also stated against a divisor.
  • Classical residue theorem on a circle; Jordan's lemma; Painlevé removability across a line; FTC along a contour.

Complex analysis / conformal mapping

  • Riemann mapping theorem — every simply connelomorphic to the disc; with the extremal-problem construction, the Koebe square-root step, and uniqueness.
  • Schwarz lemma (plus a strict form) and Schwainitesimal version — holomorphic self-maps ofthe disc contract the hyperbolic metric.
  • Schwarz reflection principle, in four forms:affine line, a circle, and an analytic arc.
  • Rouché's theorem, Hurwitz's theorem, Montel's selection theorem (normal families), Vitali's convergence theorem.
  • Classification of disc automorphisms — a holng 0 is a rotation; the general ones are theMöbius factors.

Probability / exchangeability

  • de Finetti's theorem and the de Finetti–Ryll exchangeable (indeed contractable) sequence isa mixture of i.i.d. sequences, with the directing measure identified as the conditional law of each coordinate.
  • Hewitt–Savage zero-one law — the exchangeablequence is trivial.
  • Lévy's downward theorem on an eventually constant filtration.

Positive-definite functions and semigroups

  • Bochner's theorem — continuous positive-defi Fourier transforms of finite positive measures.

  • Bernstein's theorem — completely monotone functions are exactly Laplace transforms of measures (with the Chafaï
    approximating-measure route and tightness).

  • The positive-definite function ↔ kernel correspondence, and Kolmogorov decomposition.

PDE

  • Gårding's inequality — coercivity of diverger uniform ellipticity.
  • Harnack's inequality on a planar disk.

Operator theory

  • Atkinson's theorem — an operator is Fredholmlo compacts, via parametrices; with stabilityunder small and finite-rank perturbations.

Representation theory

  • Artin–Wedderburn for group algebras — the Weon of a finite group algebra into matrixalgebras.
  • Gabriel's theorem machinery — quiver reflect, sinks/sources.
  • Weyl group generated by simple reflections, with inversion sets.

Knot theory / Heegaard Floer

  • Alexander and Maslov gradings for grid statehe grid (Cromwell) moves — the combinatorialroute to knot Floer homology.

Number theory (the one roadmap already declared complete: Effective bounds)

  • Effective counting results feeding Hermite–Mmials of bounded degree and coefficients,root-set unions, ideal counts, class-number and discriminant bounds.

Notable definitions

  • Generalized winding number (Hungerbühler–Wasem Def 2.1) with its real bounded-integrand formula — the object that
    makes the residue theorem work on-curve.

  • Cauchy principal value of a contour integral, at a point and on a set.

  • Poincaré/hyperbolic distance on the disc andression, with the triangle inequality.
  • Completely monotone functions and Bernstein functions, with closure properties.
  • Positive-definite functions on an involutivep-group positive-definite functions.
  • Directing measure and MixedIID — the de Finetti mixture representation.
  • Fredholm operators with index, adjoints, spl
  • Young tableaux, Young subgroups, permutation modules, Young symmetrizers — the Schur–Weyl toolkit.
  • Grid diagrams and the grid J-function; the standard unknot grid.
So I guess we could automate it so that whats in these bullet points was getting posted here on some regular basis as they appear in Tau Ceti?

Here's a proposal for progress reports.

Each roadmap directory at TauCetiRoadmap gets a STATUS.md and a PROGRESS.md file.

STATUS.md contains a heading saying "This file documents the status of roadmap ZZZ up until <timestamp>, commit SHA NNNN. Note that there may have been subsequent updates." and then an AI generated / updated account of which parts of the roadmap have been completed (and perhaps a brief account of the "frontier", i.e. the next steps in the roadmap past what has been completed).

It gets completely rewritten each time we update it: no history / war stories are recorded here, it's always a snapshot.

PROGRESS.md is an append only log, consisting of sections beginning: "We have made the following progress on roadmap ZZZ after <timestamp1>/<sha1>, up until <timestamp2>/<sha2>." and then an informal summary (at most a few paragraphs?). We probably should discourage the agent writing this to avoid mentioning every PR from the period separately (perhaps they can be listed at the end), and instead aim for a holistic summary, or the highlights.

We add a zulip topic "Progress logs", which automatically receives a post each time a section is added to an PROGRESS.md.

We add a new worker type (like a review worker), hooked into ./tauceti which:

  • Checks if no PROGRESS.md / STATUS.md has been updated in the last 24 hours (we can vary that number as the project grows). If so, it's time to write an update!
  • Pick the roadmap which has seen the most PRs since its STATUS.md was last updated.
  • Collect all the PRs (descriptions, content), and send these to an AI agent to write a new section for PROGRESS.md and update STATUS.md

I think this would result in keeping this documentation up to date, in reasonable size chunks (i.e. each update would probably cover 10-100 PRs at current pace?), and could be entirely automated by the existing workers.
(Sorry, @Chris Birkbeck, I was writing that as your message were appearing, I'm not ignoring you! :-)
On simple combination of these ideas is to ask the agents writing progress reports to emphasise / highlight named theorems.
That sounds good :)

But I agree a steady stream of 1 line reports about "named things that have landed" could be nice. The trick is making it selective. Otherwise we will just get an obscure post for every PR, trying to shoehorn the content into a "name".

But if you have an idea for a prompt that, given a PR, would decide whether or not it achieved a "named theorem", and either gave a one line summary or declined, I'd be interested.

(However, that requires running an agent for every single PR, whereas my proposal just runs an agent once a day.)

Examples: Chris is claiming that we have Cauchy's integral formula and the residue theorem, the Riemann mapping theorem, Harnack's inequality, definition of the Weyl group, the Poincare disc model with distance, and Fredholm operators. I didn't know any of this. For me, this is a big deal. I suspect that there are many people in this community who would be interested in that brief summary and who are completely unaware that it is happening. How are they supposed to know this sort of thing at a glance? The Tau Ceti PR's thread is unreadable and makes no distinction between what is incremental and what is important.
